A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A-D. Renamed and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original heat-diffusion simulations, MeshPDE experiments, and WeatherBench2 forecasting results in Section 6 and appendices B-D.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds a baseline comparison, component ablations, and further smoothness analyses.

M1.justification: The Taylor truncation formula, zero padding, unitary mesh convolutions, GroupSort, and unconstrained readout remain unchanged. Sections 5.2-5.3 rename encoder-decoder components as compositional smoothness-breaking components; the additional truncation-selection explanation elaborates an existing suggestion.

E1.justification: Both versions use simulated heat grids, the same PyVista meshes for heat, wave, and Cahn-Hilliard prediction, and WeatherBench2 T850/Z500 forecasting. The added analyses reuse this coverage; the MeshPDE terminology does not introduce a new dataset.

E2.justification: v2 adds MeshGraphNet as an evaluated comparator for all three MeshPDE equations in Appendix C.7, Table 5. Pfaff et al. (2021) was cited in v1 but this comparator was not benchmarked there. Existing comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: The added experiments substantially expand controlled evaluation: trained graph models are compared across truncation orders, and mesh experiments vary convolution type, dimension lifting, activation, and readout depth/width. Appendix C.6 also introduces evaluation through distributions of 2-hop neighborhood Rayleigh quotients. Retained benchmark protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's truncation sweep examined initialization; v2 adds downstream training sensitivity in Figure 9. Appendix C.8 adds direct tests of unitary layers, zero padding, activation, and readout architecture, while C.6 reports a new local-smoothness analysis, substantially extending the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run heat-grid ensembles, ten-run averages for initialization sensitivity, and MeshPDE standard deviations over meshes and initializations. Added results extend these reporting practices without changing retained replication counts or introducing new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark, multiscale-smoothness, and weather table values are unchanged. New Table 5 reports heat NRMSE of 108.1±3.2 for MeshGraphNet versus 51.9±3.6 for R-UniMesh; Table 6 reports 416.9±14.3 after replacing unitary layers with unconstrained GCNs. Further ablation results, truncation curves, and local-smoothness findings substantially expand the reported outcomes.

T1.justification: v2 adds explicit target-relative oversmoothing/undersmoothing definitions and the local 2-hop Rayleigh measure. Appendix A.6 corrects the norm-preservation argument from skew-symmetric to skew-Hermitian. The main approximation bound, mesh-preservation corollary, assumptions, and proof structure remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory contributions, and substantive conclusion retain the claims about unitary approximation limits, relaxed graph/mesh convolutions, and strong diffusive-PDE performance. Additional supporting experiments and future-work directions do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds explanations involving oscillatory wave smoothness and sharp local Cahn-Hilliard structure, plus practical requirements for computing the theoretical bound. Appendix B.2 proposes gradient stability as another explanation for unitary-network benefits, and C.6/C.8 interpret the new local-smoothness and component results.

D1.justification: Appendix C.8 specifies the preferred three-layer, width-64 readout and documents component settings. Hyperparameter and diagnostic access instructions now point more explicitly to GitHub configurations and visualizations. The abstract already linked the same repository in v1; hardware and general training budgets are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Fesser et al. (2026), Bronstein et al. (2021), and Xiao et al. (2018). Section 5.2 also acknowledges that Kiani et al. (2024) had hypothesized zero padding and distinguishes it from learned feature maps. The broader related-work positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: The revision consistently renames the encoder-decoder terminology and appendix dataset headings, adds an appendix contents list, and expands the conclusion into a Discussion section. Sample initializations move to C.9. Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a ten-panel truncation figure and the substantial baseline/ablation table block in Tables 5-10. It redraws Figure 2 with revised terminology and dimension labels, groups Table 2 columns by architecture type, and relocates initialization tables. Existing empirical plots and qualitative images are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct tests of key R-UniMesh design choices. The component ablations and trained truncation sweep in C.8 and B.2 address this substantial evidential gap, while the MeshGraphNet comparison strengthens validation of the heat-diffusion advantage. New mechanism explanations and limitations improve interpretation. Architectural-insensitivity claims remain too broad for the large wave degradations in Tables 8 and 10, but the added controls and clearer qualifications provide a substantial net improvement.
